titleEn: Dog Bite to the Forearm - Elderly Patient on an Anticoagulant

patient.name: Evelyn Harper
patient.affectEn: alert, tearful and anxious, mainly about what will happen to the dog; sitting at the kitchen table holding a blood-soaked tea towel around her left forearm; keeps saying the dog did not mean it and asking you not to let them take him away; wears hearing aids in both ears and hears you best when you face her and speak clearly
patient.speechEn: full sentences, polite, a little shaky; answers what she is asked. When going to hospital is first raised she says: "Can you just bandage it up? My son can drive me tomorrow." She agrees to go once the risks are explained in plain language (infection from a bite, the blood thinner, possible tendon damage, her tetanus being out of date) and her son is involved.

scene.settingEn: Single-storey house in Saanich at 1610 hrs. Private home, good lighting, clear path from the kitchen to the front door. The patient is at the kitchen table; there is blood on the floor and on the table, perhaps 200 mL in total. One patient. Victoria General Hospital is 15 minutes away.
hazardsEn: two dogs in the home: the son's German Shepherd that bit her, and her own small terrier - the scene is safe only once the son confirms the Shepherd is in the back yard behind a closed and latched door and the terrier is shut in a bedroom
blood on the kitchen floor and table - slip and blood-exposure hazard

bystanders.knowsEn: Answers only what is asked. If asked about the dogs: the German Shepherd is in the fenced back yard behind a closed and latched door, and the small terrier is shut in a bedroom. The Shepherd is his dog, has lived with his mother for a year, is up to date on its shots and is not a stray. It went for her terrier over a bone at about 1600 and she reached in to separate them. She did not fall. He called 911 because the bleeding would not stop; dispatch has notified the police, who will pass it to animal control. He can help reassure her, can bring her medications, and will come to the hospital with her.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: gauze, pressure dressings and trauma dressings
oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
PCP only: IV start kit with normal saline, ondansetron, dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine

dispatchEn: 1610 hrs. Code 2 to a single-storey house in Saanich. A 78-year-old woman was bitten on the left forearm by her son's German Shepherd while trying to separate it from her own small dog. Her son called and says the bleeding 'will not stop'. Victoria General Hospital is 15 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: En-route update: the son says he has put the German Shepherd outside in the fenced back yard and the door is closed. The patient is anxious, mainly about what will happen to the dog. Dispatch has notified the police, who will pass it to animal control.
arrivalEn: You pull up at a single-storey house in Saanich. The son meets you at the front door and holds it open - his mother is in the kitchen.
firstLookEn: An elderly woman sits at the kitchen table, alert and tearful, talking in full sentences. A blood-soaked tea towel is wrapped around her left forearm. There is blood on the floor and on the table, perhaps 200 mL in total. She does not have the pallor of major blood loss. Good lighting, clear path back to the door.

primary.locEn: Alert and oriented; upset and tearful but answers appropriately. (AVPU = A.)
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 18, unlaboured; chest clear with equal air entry.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 92 at the right wrist, IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR (chronic atrial fibrillation), normal strength. Bleeding from the left forearm under the towel - see the RBS.
primary.rbsEn: When the tea towel is lifted: steady VENOUS oozing from four puncture wounds and two lacerations (3 cm and 5 cm) on the LEFT forearm, plus a 6 x 4 cm skin flap avulsed on the back of the forearm, still attached at its base. It slows and stops with direct pressure over gauze and elevation (a pressure dressing holds it). There is NO arterial spurting and NO indication for a tourniquet. RIGHT forearm: two superficial skin tears from the dog's paws. LEFT shin: a bruise. Head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis and back: no injury. She did not fall and did not hit her head - no indication for spinal precautions. Left hand: distal pulse, capillary refill, movement and sensation all normal. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: warm, dry, slightly pale.

history.ccEn: The dog bit my arm and it won't stop bleeding. Please don't let them take him away - he didn't mean it.

opqrst.oEn: Around four o'clock. The big dog went for my little terrier over a bone, and I reached in with both hands to pull them apart. He got my arm.
opqrst.pEn: It's worse when my arm hangs down.
opqrst.rEn: It stays in my left forearm.
opqrst.tEn: Since he bit me, around four. It's been throbbing ever since.

history.painScoreEn: 6 out of 10, throbbing, worse when the arm hangs down (after she has used Entonox: 3 out of 10)

sample.sEn: My arm hurts and it's been bleeding. And I'm upset about the dog. Nothing else.
sample.mEn: Apixaban, 5 milligrams twice a day, for my heart rhythm. Metoprolol and amlodipine. And I took some Tylenol this afternoon for my arthritis. (Only if asked when or how much: "Two extra-strength - 1000 milligrams - at three o'clock.")
sample.pEn: Atrial fibrillation - six years now. Kidney disease, stage 3, the doctor says. High blood pressure. Arthritis and osteoporosis. (Only if asked about tetanus: "Oh... sometime in my sixties, I think.")
sample.lEn: Tea and toast at about three o'clock.
sample.eEn: The big dog went for my little terrier over a bone. I reached in with both hands to pull them apart and he got my arm. I didn't fall and I didn't hit my head. He's my son's dog - he's had all his shots, my son says. He's not a bad dog, he's not a stray.

fe.generalEn: I live on my own here. I do my own shopping and cooking. No, I haven't lost any weight.
fe.cnsEn: No dizziness. I haven't had a fall in the last year. I didn't black out today.
fe.cardiovascularEn: I've had the atrial fibrillation for six years - I'm on a blood thinner for it. No chest pain. My ankles swell a bit in the evening.
fe.giGuEn: Everything's normal. No black stools and no blood in my urine.
fe.integumentaryEn: I bruise very easily, and I get skin tears from the smallest knock.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Arthritis in both hands, and osteoporosis. I use a cane when I'm outside.
fe.endocrineEn: I'm not diabetic, and my thyroid is normal.
fe.eentEn: I wear hearing aids in both ears, and glasses for reading.

findings.headNeckEn: No injury. Hearing aids in place in both ears.
findings.chestLungsEn: Clear with equal air entry on both sides; irregular heart rhythm.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft and non-tender in all four quadrants.
findings.backEn: No injury - she did not fall.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: A 5 cm bruise on the left shin; pedal pulses present; she can bear weight normally.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: LEFT forearm: four puncture wounds, a 3 cm and a 5 cm laceration, and a 6 x 4 cm avulsed skin flap on the back of the forearm, still attached at its base and viable; oozing has stopped under the dressing (dry, no strike-through on recheck); radial pulse present, capillary refill 2 seconds, full finger movement, sensation intact. RIGHT forearm: two superficial skin tears from the dog's paws.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline (scenario time 1622, seated at the table, arm dressed and elevated)
en route, arm elevated (scenario time 1636, after Entonox): stable; dressing dry with no strike-through

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: The tea towel on her forearm is soaked through now and blood is dripping onto the floor.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan: confirm the dog is secured before entry, then bleeding control, wound care, analgesia and a full geriatric assessment
triggers: make sure the dog is locked up

expected.actionEn: Anticipate an anticoagulated elderly patient: bleeding that is slow to stop, fragile skin, and the need to ask about blood thinners early
triggers: she may be on blood thinners
bleeding will be slow to stop

expected.actionEn: Anticipate the animal hazard and blood exposure; gloves and eye protection before entering
Confirm both dogs are secured behind a closed door BEFORE entering - a bitten dog owner's home is an animal hazard until proven otherwise
Verbalize hazards (dogs, blood on the floor), environment (private home, clear exit path), MOI (dog bite while separating two animals) and one patient
triggers: hazards are the dogs and the blood on the floor

expected.actionEn: First look: alert elderly woman, upset but talking in full sentences, no pallor of major blood loss, blood-soaked dressing on the left forearm
triggers: looking at her from the doorway

expected.actionEn: Introduce yourself facing her, speak clearly - she wears hearing aids - and address her fear about the dog before you start hurting her arm
triggers: facing her so she can hear

expected.actionEn: Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert and oriented
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Assess airway
triggers: she's talking so her airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing
Assess circulation and identify the irregularly irregular pulse as chronic atrial fibrillation, not a new problem
triggers: check the rhythm of the pulse

expected.actionEn: Control the bleeding by escalating appropriately: direct pressure over gauze, then a pressure dressing, then elevation of the limb - no tourniquet is indicated for controllable venous bleeding
Complete the rapid body survey - elderly patients often have a second injury they have not mentioned; ask specifically whether she fell
Note skin: warm, dry, slightly pale
Oxygen is not indicated - she has no altered LOC, no respiratory distress and no evidence of shock; say so rather than applying it reflexively
Position of comfort, seated, with the injured arm supported and elevated
Categorize as non-RTC / stable with a 30-minute package time, and say why she still does not meet any unstable criteria
Ready to load within 30 minutes, with the wound properly dressed rather than rushed
Address the reluctance to go: explain infection risk, the anticoagulant, possible tendon injury and tetanus, involve the son, obtain consent and document the conversation
triggers: you need to go to the hospital
your tetanus is out of date

expected.actionEn: Confirm the chief complaint
HxC/C: which animal, whose dog, vaccination status, whether it was provoked, time of the bite, how much blood was lost before you arrived, and specifically whether she fell during the struggle
triggers: did you fall during the struggle
how much blood did you lose

expected.actionEn: Pain score
PMHx including atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease and tetanus status - each one changes a drug decision in this call
triggers: when was your last tetanus shot

expected.actionEn: Medications: the apixaban AND the exact time and dose of the Tylenol she has already taken today
triggers: have you taken any painkillers today
what time did you take the Tylenol

expected.actionEn: Allergies: penicillin - relevant because dog bites are usually treated with a penicillin-family antibiotic
Last oral intake
GCS with all three components
Blood pressure on the uninjured right arm - never on the bitten limb
Pulse rate, strength and rhythm - document the irregular rhythm and link it to the atrial fibrillation and the anticoagulant
Respirations
Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils
SpO2 on the uninjured hand
Temperature - a baseline matters in a contaminated wound that may become infected
Complete baseline vitals BEFORE starting any analgesia protocol
FE - General health including independence and function at home
triggers: do you manage on your own

expected.actionEn: FE - CNS including falls in the last year
triggers: any falls in the last year

expected.actionEn: FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular (atrial fibrillation on apixaban)
triggers: how long have you had atrial fibrillation

expected.actionEn: FE - GI/GU including any sign of occult bleeding on the anticoagulant
FE - Integumentary (easy bruising and fragile skin)
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (hearing aids - speak facing her)
Head and neck examination
Chest examination with auscultation
Abdominal examination
Back examination - confirm there was no fall and no unreported second injury
Upper extremities: count and describe every wound on BOTH arms, and check circulation, movement and sensation distal to the injury
Lower extremities including the shin bruise and weight bearing
Wound management skill: gentle sterile saline irrigation, flap replaced anatomically, sterile non-adherent dressing, secured without tape on fragile skin
Elevate the limb, apply cold only with intact distal circulation, and recheck the dressing for strike-through in an anticoagulated patient
triggers: cold only if circulation is intact

expected.actionEn: Rule out each analgesic out loud: acetaminophen contraindicated (dose at 1500), ibuprofen contraindicated (apixaban), methoxyflurane contraindicated (chronic kidney disease)
triggers: no acetaminophen because she had Tylenol at 1500
no ibuprofen because of the apixaban
no Penthrox because of her kidneys

expected.actionEn: Offer Entonox, which has no contraindication in this patient: self-administered, cylinder inverted three times, area ventilated, with reassessment of the pain score
Document the dog's vaccination status and ownership and confirm that police or animal control have been notified - it is a reportable bite
Handle her fragile skin deliberately: minimal tape, gentle handling, and no dragging her by the forearms during the transfer
triggers: don't pull her by the arms

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs after the transfer to the cot and after loading
Second complete set of vitals within 15 minutes for a non-priority patient
Recheck the dressing for strike-through and the distal circulation, movement and sensation after every move
Reassess the pain score after the Entonox and document the effect
Keep her warm and keep talking to her about the dog and what happens next - anxiety management is patient care
triggers: the dog will be looked after
your son can come with us

expected.actionEn: Recognize that a priority notification is not required, and give the routine arrival report per local practice
Complete hand-off including anticoagulation, the acetaminophen taken at 1500, the penicillin allergy, tetanus status and the dog's details
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes describing each wound, the analgesia reasoning and the reporting of the bite

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate walks into the house or approaches the patient before asking the son whether the dogs are secured (relying only on the dispatch update is not confirmation); asking at the door first and then entering is correct and must NOT be recorded
candidate gives Entonox without verbalizing inverting the cylinder (3 times) before use
candidate applies (or tells someone to apply) a tourniquet to the bitten arm - the bleeding is venous and is controlled by direct pressure and elevation
candidate cuts off, removes or discards the avulsed skin flap instead of laying it back in its anatomical position
candidate secures the dressings with tape stuck directly onto her skin instead of a tubular or roller bandage
candidate closes, glues, steri-strips or packs the bite wounds
candidate puts the BP cuff on, or takes the blood pressure on, the bitten left arm
candidate (or helpers on instruction) pulls, lifts or drags her by the forearms or hands during the transfer to the cot
candidate accepts her request to 'just bandage it up' and go tomorrow - plans to leave her at home or has her sign a refusal - without explaining the infection, bleeding, tendon and tetanus risks

candidate applies supplemental oxygen by non-rebreather or nasal cannula although SpO2 is 96% or higher on room air with no distress, without a titration rationale (the Entonox mouthpiece is NOT oxygen therapy)
candidate takes manual c-spine control, applies a hard collar or immobilizes her on a spinal device although she did not fall and has no spinal indication

drugs.doseEn: self-administered by inhalation, titrated to effect; INDICATED in this scenario; invert the cylinder 3 times before use; ventilate the treatment area (vehicle ventilation on in the ambulance); only after the primary survey, the pain assessment and a baseline set of vitals including SpO2
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin used in the last 5 minutes - none present in this patient
drugs.cautionsEn: shock; abdominal distention; depressant drugs; COPD; facial injuries - none present

drugs.doseEn: 500-1000 mg PO per guideline - CONTRAINDICATED in this scenario: she took 1000 mg at 1500, inside the 4-hour interval (record only if actually given)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity; severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease; acetaminophen within the past 4 hours from all sources or over the daily maximum; suspected overdose

drugs.doseEn: 300-400 mg PO per guideline - CONTRAINDICATED in this scenario: she takes apixaban, an anticoagulant (record only if actually given)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: hypersensitivity to ibuprofen or other NSAIDs; active GI hemorrhage or ulcers; pregnancy; anticoagulants

drugs.doseEn: 3 mL self-administered via inhaler, may repeat after 20 minutes, maximum 6 mL - CONTRAINDICATED in this scenario: chronic kidney disease stage 3 is clinically significant renal impairment (record only if actually given)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: under 18 years; pregnancy or breast-feeding; inadequate understanding or lack of cooperation; decreased level of consciousness or head injury; clinically significant renal impairment; liver dysfunction after halogenated anesthetics; tetracycline antibiotics; malignant hyperthermia; muscular dystrophy

drugs.doseEn: PCP only: 4 mg PO for moderate to severe nausea and vomiting - NOT indicated: she has no nausea
PCP only: 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg IM or IV for nausea, vomiting or vertigo - NOT indicated: no nausea, not a treatment for anxiety, and elderly is a listed caution
PCP only: 25-50 mg IV or PO for allergic reactions or motion sickness - NOT indicated: not a treatment for anxiety

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You did your rapid body survey - what did you find on her other arm and her legs?

trackNotes.emrEn: Every intervention this patient needs is EMR scope; the exam value is drug reasoning. Direct pressure, a pressure dressing, elevation, saline irrigation, flap replacement, non-adherent dressings secured without tape, cold, and gentle handling of fragile skin are EMR wound care. Acetaminophen, ibuprofen and methoxyflurane are in the EMR formulary and all three are contraindicated in THIS patient (acetaminophen 1000 mg at 1500, apixaban, chronic kidney disease); Entonox is indicated - say why for each one. Out of scope: an IV, ondansetron, dimenhydrinate or diphenhydramine. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds vascular access only if it were needed (it is not in a stable patient with controlled bleeding) and completes the 9-system Functional Enquiry, which is worth doing thoroughly in a geriatric patient. A PCP could give ondansetron if she became nauseated from the Entonox; she is not nauseated in this scenario. The wound care and the analgesia reasoning are identical: the same three drugs are ruled out at both licence levels and Entonox is the analgesic.

sourcePages: Scenario etr-12 (data/practical/emr-trauma-2.json): dispatch, scene (dogs must be confirmed secured), primary, transport (non-RTC; reluctance to go), history, vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions (analgesia reasoning), ongoing, handoff, criticalPitfallsEn. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (none met), p.11 Primary Survey Interventions (oxygen indications; c-spine indications), p.19 Wound Care (hemorrhage control in order of preference: direct pressure, pressure dressing, elevation, positioning, tourniquet; clean and dress minor wounds; cold only if distal circulation is not impaired), p.25 Spinal Management, p.48 Nausea-Vomiting (ondansetron and dimenhydrinate are PCP interventions), p.55 Anaphylaxis (diphenhydramine is a PCP intervention), p.58 Acetaminophen (not within 4 hours of a previous dose from all sources), p.63 Dimenhydrinate (caution: elderly), p.64 Diphenhydramine, p.65 Entonox (indication: isolated extremity injuries; contraindications; before use: primary survey, pain investigated, baseline vitals including SpO2, invert cylinder 3 times, ventilation), p.68 Ibuprofen (contraindication: anticoagulants), p.71 Methoxyflurane (contraindication: clinically significant renal impairment), p.75 Ondansetron.
